title: Solving Second-Order ODEs Using Variation of Parameters
text:
Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions [MATH: y_1(x)] and [MATH: y_2(x)]. Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution [MATH: y_p] may be written as [MATH: y_{p}(x)|= u_{1}(x)y_{1}(x) + u_{2}(x)y_{2}(x),] where [MATH: u_1] and [MATH: u_2] satisfy the following system: [MATH: {u_{1}^{′}y_{1}^{′} + u_{2}^{′}y_{2}^{′} = f(x); u_{1}^{′}y_{1} + u_{2}^{′}y_{2} = 0]

The solution to this system is [MATH: u_1(x) = -\int \dfrac{f(x)y_2(x)}{W(y_1,y_2)}\,dx, \qquad u_2(x) = \int \dfrac{f(x)y_1(x)}{W(y_1,y_2)}\,dx,] where [MATH: W(y_1,y_2)] is the Wronskian.

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is [MATH: y_c(x) = A e^{x} + B x e^{x}.] Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are [MATH: y_1(x) = e^{x}, \qquad y_2(x) = x e^{x}.]

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian: [MATH: W(y_{1}, y_{2})|=|y_{1}|y_{2}; y_{1}^{′}|y_{2}^{′}|; = y_{1}y_{2}^{′} − y_{1}^{′}y_{2}; = (e^{x})(xe^{x})^{′} − (e^{x})^{′}(xe^{x}); = (e^{x})(e^{x} + xe^{x}) − (e^{x})(xe^{x}); = e^{2x} + xe^{2x} − xe^{2x}; = e^{2x} ≠ 0]

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions [MATH: y_1(x)] and [MATH: y_2(x)] are independent.

Now compute [MATH: u_1(x)] and [MATH: u_2(x)]: [MATH: u_{1}(x)|= − ∫(18xe^{x} ⋅ xe^{x})/(e^{2x})dx; = − 18∫x^{2}dx; = − 6x^{3}; u_{2}(x)|= ∫(18xe^{x} ⋅ e^{x})/(e^{2x})dx; = 18∫xdx; = 9x^{2}]

Therefore, the particular solution is [MATH: y_{p}(x)|= u_{1}y_{1} + u_{2}y_{2}; = (− 6x^{3})e^{x} + (9x^{2})(xe^{x}); = − 6x^{3}e^{x} + 9x^{3}e^{x}; = 3x^{3}e^{x}.]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows: [MATH: y(x)|= y_{c}(x) + y_{p}(x); = Ae^{x} + Bxe^{x} + 3x^{3}e^{x}_(⏟)_(g(x))]

Therefore, we conclude that [MATH: g(x) = 3x^3 e^{x}.]

title: Solving Second-Order ODEs Using Variation of Parameters
text:
Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions [MATH: y_1(x)] and [MATH: y_2(x).] Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution [MATH: y_p] using the ansatz [MATH: y_{p}(x)|= u_{1}(x)y_{1}(x) + u_{2}(x)y_{2}(x),] where [MATH: u_1] and [MATH: u_2] satisfy the following system: [MATH: {u_{1}^{′}y_{1}^{′} + u_{2}^{′}y_{2}^{′} = f(x); u_{1}^{′}y_{1} + u_{2}^{′}y_{2} = 0]

The solution to this system is [MATH: u_1(x)=-\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f(x)y_2(x)}{W(y_1,y_2)}\,\mathrm{d}x, \qquad u_2(x)=\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f(x)y_1(x)}{W(y_1,y_2)}\,\mathrm{d}x,] where [MATH: W(y_1,y_2)] is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is [MATH: f(x)=\tan x.]

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is [MATH: y_c(x)=A\cos x + B\sin x.]

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are [MATH: y_1(x)=\cos x, \qquad y_2(x)=\sin x.]

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are linearly independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian: [MATH: W(y_{1}, y_{2})|=|y_{1}|y_{2}; y_{1}^{′}|y_{2}^{′}|; = y_{1}(x)y_{2}^{′}(x) − y_{1}^{′}(x)y_{2}(x); = (\cos x)(\sin x)^{′} − (\cos x)^{′}(\sin x); = (\cos x)(\cos x) − (− \sin x)(\sin x); = \cos^{2} x + \sin^{2} x; = 1 ≠ 0]

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions [MATH: y_1(x)] and [MATH: y_2(x)] are independent.

Let’s compute [MATH: u_1(x)] and [MATH: u_2(x)]: [MATH: u_{1}(x)|= − ∫(f(x)y_{2}(x))/(W(y_{1}, y_{2}))dx; = − ∫\tan x\sin xdx; = \sin x − \ln|\tan x + \sec x|; u_{2}(x)|= ∫(f(x)y_{1}(x))/(W(y_{1}, y_{2}))dx; = ∫\tan x\cos xdx; = ∫\sin xdx; = − \cos x]

Therefore, the particular solution is [MATH: y_{p}(x)|= u_{1}y_{1} + u_{2}y_{2}; = (\cos x)(\sin x − \ln|\tan x + \sec x|) + (− \cos x)(\sin x); = − \cos x\ln|\tan x + \sec x|.]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows: [MATH: y(x)|= y_{c}(x) + y_{p}(x); = A\cos x + B\sin x− \cos x\ln|\tan x + \sec x|_(⏟)_(g(x))]

Therefore, we conclude that [MATH: g(x)=-\cos x\ln\!\left|\tan x+\sec x\right|.]

title: Linear Differential Operators
text: • First, let's consider the following differential operator: [MATH: D_1(y) = x\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} +x^2y] This operator is indeed linear. To see this, we need to check that the linearity condition above holds. So we start by applying our operator to the function [MATH: y = a y_1(x) + b y_2(x){:}] [MATH: D_{1}(ay_{1} + by_{2}) = x(d)/(dx)(ay_{1} + by_{2}) + x^{2}(ay_{1} + by_{2})] Since derivatives distribute over sums, and [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are constants, we have [MATH: D_{1}(ay_{1} + by_{2})|= x(d)/(dx)(ay_{1}) + x(d)/(dx)(by_{2}) + x^{2}(ay_{1} + by_{2}); = ax(d)/(dx)(y_{1}) + bx(d)/(dx)(y_{2}) + ax^{2}y_{1} + bx^{2}y_{2}; = a(x(dy_{1})/(dx) + x^{2}y_{1})_(⏟)_(D_{1}(y_{1})) + b(x(dy_{2})/(dx) + x^{2}y_{2})_(⏟)_(D_{1}(y_{2}))] Thus, since [MATH: D_1(ay_1 + by_2) = aD_1(y_1) + bD_1(y_2),] the operator [MATH: D_1] is linear.

title: Equations of Lines in Standard Form
text:
The standard form equation of a line is

[MATH: ax+by=c,]

where

  • [MATH: a,b,] and [MATH: c] are all integers,

  • [MATH: a\geq 0,] and

  • [MATH: a,b,] and [MATH: c] have no common factors greater than [MATH: 1.]

With that in mind, let's examine our equations.

  • Equation I is not in standard form because the coefficient of [MATH: x] is negative ([MATH: -5]).

  • Equation II is in standard form. Indeed, the variables are on the left-hand side, while the constant term is on the right-hand side: [MATH: \underbrace{3x- y}_{\textrm{variables}} \quad = \underbrace{\phantom{y}-2\phantom{y}}_{\textrm{constant}}] All coefficients are integers (namely, [MATH: 3,] [MATH: -1,] and [MATH: -2]) and don't have common factors greater than [MATH: 1.] Also, the coefficient of [MATH: x] is positive ([MATH: 3]).

  • Equation III is in standard form. Indeed, the variables are on the left-hand side, while the constant term is on the right-hand side: [MATH: \underbrace{3x}_{\textrm{variables}} \quad = \underbrace{\phantom{y}5\phantom{y}}_{\textrm{constant}}] All coefficients are integers (namely, [MATH: 3] and [MATH: 5]) and don't have common factors greater than [MATH: 1.] Also, the coefficient of [MATH: x] is positive ([MATH: 3]).

  • Equation IV is not in standard form because the coefficients [MATH: (2,-6,] and [MATH: 4)] have a common factor of [MATH: 2.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

title: Simplifying Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Tangent

title: Proving Inequalities Using Induction
text:
The principle of induction states the following: Suppose we have a sequence of mathematical statements [MATH: P(1), P(2), P(3),\ldots,] where

  • [MATH: P(1)] is true, and

  • [MATH: P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1)] for every [MATH: k\in\mathbb N.]

Then, [MATH: P(n)] is true for every [MATH: n\in\mathbb N.]

In this case, the general statement [MATH: P(n)] we're required to prove is the following:

[MATH: n^2 > 2n+2 \quad\text{for}\quad n \geq 3.]

We start by proving the so-called base case. Since we are required to prove the statement for [MATH: n \geq 3,] the base case is [MATH: P(3).] So, we substitute [MATH: n=3] into both the left-hand side and right-hand side and show that the left-hand side is greater than the right-hand side:

We proceed using induction on [MATH: n.]

Base Case: We first prove our statement is true for the base case [MATH: n=3.] For the left-hand side, we have [MATH: 3^{2} = 9,] and for the right-hand side, we have [MATH: 2(3) + 2 = 8,] Thus, our statement is true for [MATH: n=3.]

Next, we state our inductive hypothesis. Here, we assume that the given statement is true for some [MATH: n=k\geq 3.]

Inductive Hypothesis: We assume that for some [MATH: n=k\geq 3,] we have [MATH: k^2 > 2k+2.]

We must show that [MATH: P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1).] Let's start by writing down [MATH: P(k+1).] This is the first part of the so-called inductive step.

Inductive Step: We're required to prove that [MATH: (k+1)^2 > 2(k+1)+2 . \qquad\qquad (\ast)]

The idea is to rewrite the left-hand side of [MATH: (\ast)] using the inductive hypothesis and apply algebraic techniques to show that this is greater than the right-hand side. We do this as follows:

We write [MATH: (k + 1)^{2}|= k^{2} + 2k + 1.] By the inductive hypothesis, we have [MATH: k^{2} + 2k + 1|= (k^{2})_(⏟)_(> 2k + 2) + 2k + 1; > 2k + 2 + 2k + 1; = 2k + 2 + 2k_(⏟)_(> 1) + 1; > 2(k + 1) + 2,] as required.

Since we've shown that the left-hand side of [MATH: (\ast)] is greater than the right-hand side, our proof is complete. So, let's write down our conclusion.

Therefore, by the principle of induction, [MATH: n^2 > 2n+2] for all [MATH: n \geq 3.]

title: Proving Inequalities Using Induction
text:
The principle of induction states the following: Suppose we have a sequence of mathematical statements [MATH: P(1), P(2), P(3), \ldots,] where

  • [MATH: P(1)] is true, and

  • [MATH: P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1)] for every [MATH: k \in \mathbb N.]

Then, [MATH: P(n)] is true for every [MATH: n\in\mathbb N.]

In this case, the general statement [MATH: P(n)] we're required to prove is the following: [MATH: 2^n +1 \leq 3^n \quad\text{for} \quad n \geq 1.]

We start by proving the so-called base case, [MATH: P(1).] To do this, we substitute [MATH: n = 1] into both the left-hand side and right-hand side and show that the left-hand side is less than or equal to the right-hand side:

We proceed using induction on [MATH: n.]

Base Case: We first prove our statement is true for the base case [MATH: n = 1.] For the left-hand side, we have [MATH: 2^{1} + 1 = 3,] and for the right-hand side, we have [MATH: 3^{1} = 3,] Thus, our statement is true for [MATH: n = 1.]

Next, we state our inductive hypothesis. Here, we assume that the given statement is true for some [MATH: n = k \geq 1.]

Inductive Hypothesis: We assume that for some [MATH: n = k \geq 1,] we have [MATH: 2^k +1 \leq 3^k.]

We must show that [MATH: P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1).] Let's start by writing down [MATH: P(k+1).] This is the first part of the so-called inductive step.

Inductive Step: We're required to prove that [MATH: 2^{k+1} + 1\leq 3^{k+1}. \qquad\qquad (\ast)]

The idea is to rewrite the left-hand side of [MATH: (\ast)] using the inductive hypothesis and apply algebraic techniques to show that this is less than or equal to the right-hand side. We do this as follows:

We write [MATH: 2^{k + 1} + 1|= 2^{k} ⋅ 2^{1} + 1; = 2(2^{k}) + 1; = 2^{k} + 2^{k} + 1.] By the inductive hypothesis, we have [MATH: 2^{k} + 2^{k} + 1_(⏟)_(≤ 3^{k})|≤ 2^{k} + 3^{k}; = 2^{k}_(⏟)_(< 3^{k} < 2 ⋅ 3^{k}) + 3^{k}; < 2 ⋅ 3^{k} + 3^{k}; = 3 ⋅ 3^{k}; = 3^{k + 1},] as required.

Since we've shown that the left-hand side of [MATH: (\ast)] is less than or equal to the right-hand side, our proof is complete. So, let's write down our conclusion.

Therefore, by the principle of induction, [MATH: 2^n +1 \leq 3^n] for all [MATH: n \geq 1.]

title: The Power-Reducing Formulas for Sine and Cosine
text:
Let [MATH: z = \cos\theta + \textrm{i}\sin\theta.] We start with the following identities:

[MATH: z + (1)/(z) = 2\cos θ, z^{n} + (1)/(z^{n}) = 2\cos nθ]

Raising both sides to the power [MATH: 3] in the first identity, we get [MATH: \left(z + \dfrac{1}{z}\right)^3 = (2\cos\theta)^3 =8\cos^3\theta.]

Now, we expand the binomial using the binomial theorem and simplify the result using our identities, as follows: [MATH: (z + (1)/(z))^{3}|= z^{3} + 3z^{2}((1)/(z)) + 3z((1)/(z))^{2} + ((1)/(z))^{3}; = z^{3} + 3z + 3((1)/(z)) + (1)/(z^{3}); = (z^{3} + (1)/(z^{3}))_(⏟)_(2\cos 3θ) + 3(z + (1)/(z))_(⏟)_(2\cos θ); = 2\cos 3θ + 3(2\cos θ); = 2\cos 3θ + 6\cos θ]

So, by equating [MATH: 8\cos^3\theta] with the above, we get [MATH: 8\cos^3\theta = 2\cos3\theta + 6\cos\theta.]

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by [MATH: 8,] which gives [MATH: \cos^3\theta = \frac{1}{4}\cos3\theta + \frac{3}{4}\cos\theta.]

Therefore, [MATH: B=\dfrac{3}{4}.]

Let [MATH: z = \cos\theta + \textrm{i}\sin\theta.] We start with the following identities:

[MATH: (z − (1)/(z)) = 2\textrm{i}\sin θ(z^{n} − (1)/(z^{n})) = 2\textrm{i}\sin nθ]

Raising both sides to the power [MATH: 5] in the first identity, we get [MATH: \left(z - \dfrac{1}{z}\right)^5 = (2\textrm{i}\sin\theta)^5 %=32\textrm{i}^5\sin^5\theta =32\textrm{i}\sin^5\theta \,.]

Now, we expand the binomial using the binomial theorem and simplify the result using our identities, as follows: [MATH: (z − (1)/(z))^{5}|= z^{5} − 5z^{4}((1)/(z)) + 10z^{3}((1)/(z))^{2} − 10z^{2}((1)/(z))^{3} + 5z((1)/(z))^{4} − ((1)/(z))^{5}; = z^{5} − 5z^{3} + 10z − (10)/(z) + (5)/(z^{3}) − (1)/(z^{5}); = (z^{5} − (1)/(z^{5}))_(⏟)_(2\textrm{i}\sin 5θ) − 5(z^{3} − (1)/(z^{3}))_(⏟)_(2\textrm{i}\sin 3θ) + 10(z − (1)/(z))_(⏟)_(2\textrm{i}\sin θ); = 2\textrm{i}\sin 5θ − 5(2\textrm{i}\sin 3θ) + 10(2\textrm{i}\sin θ); = 2\textrm{i}\sin 5θ − 10\textrm{i}\sin 3θ + 20\textrm{i}\sin θ]

By equating [MATH: 32\textrm{i} \sin^5 \theta] with the above, we get [MATH: 32\textrm{i}\sin^5\theta = 2\textrm{i}\sin5\theta - 10\textrm{i}\sin3\theta + 20\textrm{i}\sin\theta.]

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by [MATH: 32\textrm{i},] which gives [MATH: \sin^5\theta = \dfrac{1}{16}\sin5\theta - \dfrac{5}{16}\sin3\theta+\dfrac{5}{8}\sin\theta.]

Therefore, [MATH: A=\dfrac{1}{16}.]

title: The Power-Reducing Formulas for Sine and Cosine
text:
Let [MATH: z = \cos\theta + \textrm{i}\sin\theta.] We start with the following identities:

Therefore, [MATH: A=\dfrac{1}{8}.]

title: Combining Congruence Criteria for Triangles
text:
First, we recall the ASA (Angle-Side-Angle) congruence criterion:

Two triangles are congruent if and only if two angles and the included side of one triangle are congruent to two angles and the included side of the other triangle.

Now, we have [MATH: \underbrace{\angle A \cong \angle D}_{\textrm{Angle}}, \qquad \underbrace{\overline{AB}\cong \overline{DE}}_{\textrm{(included) Side}}, \qquad \underbrace{\angle B \cong \angle E}_{\textrm{Angle}}.]

Therefore, [MATH: \triangle ABC] and [MATH: \triangle DEF] are congruent by ASA.

title: Combining Congruence Criteria for Triangles
text:
First, we recall the SAS (Side-Angle-Side) congruence criterion:

Two triangles are congruent if and only if two sides and the included angle of one triangle are congruent to two sides and the included angle of the other triangle.

Notice that [MATH: \angle QPR \cong \angle MPN] since these two angles are vertical.

Now, we have [MATH: \underbrace{\overline{PR}\cong \overline{PN}}_{\textrm{Side}}\,, \qquad \underbrace{\angle QPR \cong \angle MPN}_{\textrm{(included) Angle}}\,, \qquad \underbrace{\overline{PQ}\cong \overline{PM}}_{\textrm{Side}}\,.]

Therefore, [MATH: \triangle PQR] and [MATH: \triangle PMN] are congruent by SAS.

title: Combining Congruence Criteria for Triangles
text:
First, we recall the HL (Hypotenuse-Leg) congruence criterion:

Two right triangles are congruent if and only if they have congruent hypotenuses and a pair of congruent legs.

Notice that the triangles have a common side, [MATH: \overline{AB}.] To determine which criterion applies, it's helpful to think of this as two separate triangles, as shown below.

Next, we have [MATH: \underbrace{m\angle{C} = m\angle{D} = 90^\circ}_{\textrm{Right angle}}\,, \qquad \underbrace{\overline{AB} \cong \overline{AB}}_{\textrm{Hypotenuse}}\,, \qquad \underbrace{\overline{BC}\cong \overline{BD}}_{\textrm{Leg}}\,.]

Therefore, [MATH: \triangle ABC] and [MATH: \triangle ABD] are congruent by HL.
